title: Complex-Multiplication Terminals for Supersingular Isogeny Path-Finding
authors: Zheng Tao, Zhi Hu, Yijing Zhang, and Changan Zhao
abstract: We propose a complementary stopping strategy based on complex multiplication (CM) for the subfield-search stage of supersingular isogeny path-finding, a bottleneck in the Delfs-Galbraith/SuperSolver algorithm.  The original search performs a non-backtracking walk in the supersingular \(2\)-isogeny graph until it reaches the subfield terminal set \(S_p\).  Our idea is to enlarge the set of recognizable terminals, by adding a precomputed set of CM supersingular vertices. For a discriminant bound \(M\), we construct \(S_{\mathrm{CM}}(M)\) from roots of Hilbert class polynomials \(H_D(X)\) over \(\mathbb F_{p^2}\),  where \(D\) ranges over inert negative fundamental discriminants with \(|D|<M\).  The walk then stops upon reaching \(S_p\cup S_{\mathrm{CM}}(M)\).  The only additional per-visit cost is an expected \(O(1)\) hash-table membership query in the precomputed CM terminal table. We estimate the size and preprocessing cost of \(S_{\mathrm{CM}}(M)\), obtaining the heuristic growth \(|S_{\mathrm{CM}}(M)|=\Theta(M^{3/2})\), and show that the overlap \(S_{\mathrm{CM}}(M)\cap S_p\) is lower order.  We also give terminal-connection procedures showing how searches that stop at CM vertices can be converted into full isogeny paths under the standard quaternionic and KLPT heuristics. The method does not change the asymptotic exponent of the underlying Delfs-Galbraith search; instead, it provides a complementary technique for existing subfield-search methods by adding efficiently recognizable CM terminals.  Experiments on small parameters show that enlarging the terminal union reduces both visited vertices and field multiplications, while lookup benchmarks at SQIsign parameters confirm that the additional table membership test has stable and moderate per-visit overhead.

        Abstract. We propose a complementary stopping strategy based on
        complex multiplication (CM) for the subfield-search stage of supersingu-
        lar isogeny path-finding, a bottleneck in the Delfs–Galbraith/SuperSolver

        a precomputed set of CM supersingular vertices. For a discriminant

1   Introduction

Given two supersingular j-invariants over Fp2 , the supersingular isogeny path
problem asks for an explicit isogeny path connecting the corresponding supersin-
gular elliptic curves. This is a central algorithmic task in isogeny-based cryptog-
raphy, underlying constructions and assumptions such as CGL-type hash func-
tions and SQIsign-type signatures [7,14]. For a small prime ℓ, the problem can be
viewed as finding paths in the supersingular ℓ-isogeny graph Gℓ , whose vertices
are supersingular j-invariants over Fp2 and whose edges correspond to cyclic
ℓ-isogenies [24,27].
    The Delfs–Galbraith algorithm and SuperSolver reduce the general path-
finding problem to a subfield search [15,11]. Starting from a supersingular vertex
in Sp2 , where Sp2 denotes the set of supersingular j-invariants over Fp2 , the
search walks in the 2-isogeny graph until it reaches the subfield subset Sp =
Sp2 ∩ Fp . Since |Sp2 | = Θ(p) whereas |Sp | = Θ(p1/2 ), the subfield target is
sparse [29,15]. Under the standard rapid-mixing heuristic, the expected number

of visited vertices before hitting Sp is therefore of order |Spp | = Θ(p1/2 ), making
this subfield search the main bottleneck in the Delfs–Galbraith framework.
    SuperSolver improves the concrete cost of this bottleneck by optimized ter-
minal detection: besides testing whether the current vertex lies in Sp , it also
detects whether small-degree neighbours lie in Sp [11]. This searches a larger
local neighbourhood per unit of work, but the recognizable terminal structure
remains tied to the subfield.
    This paper develops a complementary approach. Rather than modifying the
underlying 2-isogeny walk, we enlarge the set of efficiently recognizable termi-
nal vertices. The additional terminals come from complex multiplication (CM).
For a parameter M , our analyzed core set uses negative fundamental discrim-
inants D with |D| < M , and lets HD (X) be the corresponding Hilbert class
polynomial. The roots of HD parametrize complex elliptic curves with CM by
OD , and deg HD = h(D) is the corresponding
                                    √               class number [13]. By Deuring
reduction, when p is inert in Q( D), the roots of HD (X) over Fp2 give su-
persingular j-invariants [16,21]. We precompute these vertices as an additional
terminal set, denoted by SCM (M ) and store them in a precomputed CM terminal
table. This choice is motivated by the work of Love and Boneh on supersingular
curves with small noninteger endomorphisms [23]. Their results show that CM
vertices associated with small discriminants carry useful structural information:
same-discriminant vertices admit controlled connections, while vertices from dis-
tinct discriminants satisfy nontrivial separation bounds. We use this structure
as a source of additional recognizable terminals in the subfield-search stage. The
search phase then uses the enlarged terminal set Sp ∪ SCM (M ). At each visited
vertex, the algorithm keeps the SuperSolver subfield tests and adds one mem-
bership query in the precomputed CM terminal table. Thus the walk in G2 is
unchanged; only the stopping condition is enlarged.
    To turn this enlarged stopping rule into a complete path-finding method,
several issues must be addressed. One must estimate the size of SCM (M ) and

Our Contributions. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as
follows:

1. We introduce a CM terminal set SCM (M ) obtained from roots of Hilbert
   class polynomials HD (X) mod p, where D ranges over inert negative fun-
   damental discriminants with |D| < M . The search phase uses the enlarged
   terminal set Sp ∪ SCM (M ), while the underlying non-backtracking walk in
   G2 is unchanged. This gives a complementary stopping mechanism to the
   subfield terminals used in Delfs–Galbraith and SuperSolver.
2. We estimate the supply of CM terminal vertices using class-number sums.
   Under the inertness-frequency heuristic (H1), stated and motivated in Sec-
   tion 3.2, the raw CM supply grows as RCM (M ) = Θ(M 3/2 ). We also bound
   the subfield overlap SCM (M ) ∩ Sp , showing that its contribution is lower
   order, namely O(M
                   e   ). We further account for the preprocessing cost of con-
   structing SCM (M ) and the lookup cost of the CM terminal table, and model
   each membership query as an expected O(1) operation.
3. We give post-search procedures for connecting terminal vertices. The Delfs–
   Galbraith subfield connection applies when both lie in Sp . For CM terminals,
   we distinguish same-discriminant CM–CM, different-discriminant CM–CM,
   and mixed CM–subfield cases. Same-discriminant terminals are connected by
   a Galbraith-style bidirectional collision search, in which small split-prime-
   degree neighbours are generated directly using modular polynomials. The
   different-discriminant and mixed cases are routed through reference quater-
   nionic data and the KLPT algorithm.
4. We implement the CM-enhanced search in SageMath and Python. On small
   search parameters, enlarging the terminal union reduces both the average
   number of visited vertices and the Fp -multiplication counts. Lookup bench-
   marks at SQIsign-size parameters show that the CM table membership test
   has stable overhead, while the main practical cost lies in preprocessing and
   storage.

Supersingular isogeny graphs Let ℓ ≥ 2 be an integer with gcd(ℓ, p) = 1.
The supersingular ℓ-isogeny graph Gℓ has vertex set Sp2 , and its edges corre-
spond to cyclic ℓ-isogenies between the associated supersingular elliptic curves,
up to isomorphism. When ℓ is prime, Gℓ is connected and, away from the usual
exceptional vertices with extra automorphisms, is (ℓ + 1)-regular. These graphs
are Ramanujan and form expander families [24,27].
    In this work the search phase is performed primarily in the 2-isogeny graph
G2 . The Delfs–Galbraith algorithm searches from a given supersingular ver-
tex until it reaches Sp . Under the standard rapid-mixing heuristic for non-
backtracking walks in G2 , the expected number of visited vertices before hitting

Delfs–Galbraith algorithm and SuperSolver The Delfs–Galbraith algo-
rithm reduces the problem of connecting two supersingular vertices in Sp2 to
the problem of reaching Sp . In practice, this search is implemented as a depth-
first search (DFS) of the non-backtracking 2-isogeny tree, often with randomized
branch choices. For a full path-finding instance with two input vertices jA , jB ,
the procedure is applied to both sides, producing jA ⇝ tA , jB ⇝ tB ; tA , tB ∈ Sp .
The second phase of the Delfs–Galbraith algorithm then connects tA and tB
inside the Fp -supersingular graph.
    SuperSolver improves the terminal-detection step by avoiding full root fac-
torization of the specialized modular polynomial Φℓ (X, j), where Φℓ (X, Y ) ∈
Z[X, Y ] is the classical modular polynomial: for two j-invariants j1 , j2 , the equa-
tion Φℓ (j1 , j2 ) = 0 means that the corresponding elliptic curves are connected
by a cyclic ℓ-isogeny [4,11]. For each selected ℓ, it specializes the modular poly-
nomial at the current vertex, f (X) = Φℓ (X, j) ∈ Fp2 [X]. Writing Fp2 = Fp (β),
it decomposes f into its real and imaginary parts

                     f (X) = g1 (X) + βg2 (X), g1 , g2 ∈ Fp [X].

Then f has a root in Fp if and only if g1 and g2 have a common root over Fp . If g1
and g2 have a nonconstant greatest common divisor, then the current vertex has
an ℓ-isogenous neighbour in Sp . The search can therefore terminate by following
this ℓ-isogeny to the corresponding terminal.

Deuring correspondence and quaternionic methods Let Bp,∞ denote the
quaternion algebra over Q ramified exactly at p and at infinity. The Deuring
correspondence relates supersingular elliptic curves in characteristic p to max-
imal orders in Bp,∞ . More precisely, if E/Fp2 is supersingular, then End(E) is
isomorphic to a maximal order in Bp,∞ . Conversely, maximal orders in Bp,∞ ,
up to the appropriate equivalence, arise as endomorphism rings of supersingu-
lar elliptic curves [16,21]. In particular, when p ≡ 3 (mod 4), the supersingular
vertex j = 1728 has CM by the order of discriminant −4, and its corresponding
maximal order in Bp,∞ is explicitly known.
    Under this correspondence, separable isogenies are described by quaternionic
ideals. If two supersingular curves E1 and E2 have endomorphism rings corre-
sponding to maximal orders R1 ≃ End(E1 ), R2 ≃ End(E2 ), then an isogeny
from E1 to E2 corresponds to an ideal linking R1 and R2 , the degree of which is
given by the reduced norm of the corresponding ideal. KLPT algorithm converts
such quaternionic ideals into isogeny paths of small-prime or powersmooth de-
gree. Under their standard heuristic assumptions on the distribution of suitable
primes, these algorithms run in probabilistic polynomial time [20].

4     CM-Enhanced Search Algorithm and Complexity
This section describes the search phase of our CM-enhanced path-finding al-
gorithm. Starting from the Delfs–Galbraith/SuperSolver algorithm, we modify
the terminal tests by adding membership queries against SCM (M ), implemented
through a precomputed CM terminal table. We present the resulting bidirec-
tional search procedure, discuss the terminal cases and the corresponding path-
connection methods, and then analyze the costs introduced by the CM enhance-
ment: the lookup overhead, the effect of the enlarged terminal set on the expected
hitting time, and the post-processing cost for path connection.

This section reports implementation results for the CM-enhanced search frame-

First, we measure the overhead of membership queries in the precomputed CM

the number of visited vertices, the number of field operations, and the cost of

useful for comparison; the main implementation-independent measurements are
visited vertices and field-operation counts.

The measurements above support the two implementation assumptions behind
the CM-enhanced method. First, the CM table membership test behaves as
a stable per-visit operation: at SQIsign-size parameter levels, the lookup time
remains around 20 µs, despite the increase in table size. This supports the use
of an expected O(1) lookup cost in the search-stage model.

In the experiment isolating the stopping rule, CM terminals account for a sub-
stantial fraction of stopping events once their effective size is comparable to

ant reduces both the average number of visited vertices and the corresponding
Fp -multiplication counts across all tested parameter sets.

plementary stopping mechanism rather than a replacement for the SuperSolver
subfield tests. Its search overhead is modest and stable, while the main prac-
tical cost lies in the preprocessing and storage required to construct large CM
terminal tables.


7     Discussion
The CM-enhanced stopping rule should be viewed as a complementary mech-
anism, rather than as a replacement for existing search strategies. It does not
modify the underlying non-backtracking walk in the 2-isogeny graph G2 , nor
does it remove the subfield tests used in Delfs–Galbraith or the optimized odd-
degree probing tests used in SuperSolver. Instead, it adds an additional input-
independent source of recognizable terminal vertices, namely the precomputed
CM terminal set SCM (M ).
   It is useful to distinguish the CM terminal set from a generic meet-in-the-
middle time–space tradeoff. A meet-in-the-middle method builds an instance-
dependent collision table from one input vertex, stores the leaves together with
their paths, and then searches from the other input vertex until  a collision is

found. If N vertices are stored, the expected cost is O N + N . Balancing the

space tradeoff. The CM terminal set has a different role. It is not built from one
of the two input vertices, and it does not store paths from a specific endpoint.
Instead, it depends only on p and the discriminant bound M , and can be reused
across many independent search instances. For a single instance with the same
amount of storage, a generic meet-in-the-middle table can be more direct, since
a collision immediately provides a path through the stored tree. The purpose of
SCM (M ) is therefore not to replace meet-in-the-middle search, but to provide a
reusable arithmetic stopping source that can be combined with Delfs–Galbraith,
SuperSolver, or other search procedures.

    The main practical limitation is the size of the computable CM terminal
set. The raw CM supply grows heuristically as RCM (M ) = Θ(M 3/2 ). Thus, in
order to make |SCM (M )| comparable to |Sp | = Θ(p1/2 ), one would need roughly
M ≈ p1/3 . For cryptographic-size primes, this can be far beyond the range that is
currently practical for large-scale class-polynomial precomputation and storage.

    In our current implementation and computational environment, CM data
can be generated up to discriminants of size about 220 . This is sufficient for
the lookup benchmarks and the small search experiments reported above, but
it is far from the range required to make SCM (M ) comparable to Sp at large
cryptographic parameters. Although the computable CM range is limited, the
CM perspective still suggests a useful sanity check for concrete cryptographic
parameters. For schemes such as SQIsign, one should check whether the selected
supersingular curves lie in a low-discriminant CM family; equivalently, whether
their j-invariants occur as roots of HD (X) mod p for small fundamental discrim-
inants D. Passing such a test does not constitute a security proof, but it rules
out one class of special CM-derived curves that may be easier to recognize or
connect using the methods studied here.

    This point should be interpreted carefully. Our results do not imply an imme-
diate change in the bit-security of SQIsign-size parameters. Rather, they indicate
that low-discriminant CM structure is a concrete feature that can be tested dur-
ing parameter generation and concrete security evaluation.

    Several directions remain open. First, the construction of SCM (M ) and the
storage of the CM terminal table could be optimized, for example by using
compressed representations and memory-efficient hashing. Second, a conductor-
aware extension to non-maximal quadratic orders could also be implemented and
benchmarked, including the corresponding horizontal and vertical isogeny steps.
Third, the CM table could be combined with other search strategies, including
meet-in-the-middle methods, or local terminal tests.

    Overall, the CM-enhanced method should be understood as a reusable stop-
ping mechanism. Its value is not in replacing generic time–space tradeoffs, but
in showing that CM supersingular vertices can be organized into a precomputed
terminal set and used to complement existing subfield-search algorithms.
